# Overview

Hospital-acquired infections (HAIs), or healthcare-associated infections, are a major problem in United States hospital systems. HAIs are linked to many factors, such as the patient's age or stay at a hospital, as well as the the hospital's infrastructure (e.g. number of available beds at the hospital) and staffing. Knowing how these factors affect a patients risk of acquiring HCIs is important for hospital leaders and institutions to implement policies in minimizing the risk HCIs and better patient care. 

The main research question of this analysis is: 
How do patient and hospital factors affect the risk of a hospital-acquired infection in a hospital? 

# Data Description and Processing

The dataset contains data collected from hospitals in the United States, with each row representing one hospital.

We categorized the variables in the data set in terms of "Patient Factors" and "Hospital Factors". "Patient Factors" are variables that reference information about a patient, such as how long they stay at the hospital, and their age. "Hospital Factors" are variables associated with the hospital, such as the number of beds the hospital has and the number of nurses for staff. Additionally, we placed "Culture" and "Xray" variables under the group "Hospital Factors", as these are tests conducted by hospitals on patients.  


**Patient Factors**:

Stay (numeric): average length of patient stay (days)

Age (numeric): average patient age (years)


**Hospital Factors**:

Culture (numeric): Ratio of number of cultures (testing a patient's sample for infection-causing microorganisms) performed to number of patients without signs or symptoms of hospital-acquired infection, times 100.

Xray (numeric): Ratio of number of X-rays (taking an image of the body, particularly the chest, to look for conditions such as pneumonia) performed to number of patients without signs or symptoms of pneumonia, times 100.

Beds (numeric): Average number of beds in hospital during study period.

MedSchool (categorical - factor): Hospital has an associated medical school: 1 =Yes, 2=No --> We decided to factor this categorical variable as there are different "groups" or levels for medical school (1 is "Yes", 2 is "No"). 

Region (categorical - factor): Geographic region, where: 1 =NE, 2=NC, 3=S, 4=W --> We decided to factor this variable as there are different "groups" of regions. One group of hospitals are located in the Northeast, three distinct groups are located in North Central, South, and West in the United States. 

Census (numeric): Average number of patients in hospital per day during study period.

Nurses (numeric): Average number of full-time equivalent registered and licensed practical nurses during study period (number full-time plus one half the number part time).

Facilities (numeric): Percent of 35 potential facilities and services that are provided by the hospital.

Outcome/ Dependent Variable: 
Our dependent variable is infection risk (named InfctRsk in our dataset). 
InfctRsk (numeric): Average estimated probability of acquiring infection in hospital (percent)

The data set was checked for missing values. Of the original 116 observations, we removed 3 observations that contained missing values leaving 113 complete observations.

We used the InfctRsk (infection risk) variable as our outcome. 

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Read the dataset and set it to a dataframe 
infection.df = read.csv("dataset2.csv")

infection.df = na.omit(infection.df)

infection.df$MedSchool = factor(infection.df$MedSchool)
infection.df$Region = factor(infection.df$Region)


levels(infection.df$MedSchool) = c("Yes", "No")

```

We did not find or remove any outliers in our dataset. 

# Data Exploration

In figure 1, the distribution of the outcome variable, infection risk (named in our dataset as InfctRsk), shows an approximately normal distribution, with only one peak. We can also support that the distribution is normal as the number of observations is greater than 50 (113 > 50). The density curve fits the data pretty well. 


```{r, echo=FALSE}
hist(infection.df$InfctRsk, freq = FALSE, # freq = FALSE for density scale on y-axis
     main = "Histogram of Infection Risk Variable", # turn off the title as using the fig.cap
     xlab = "Infection Risk (%)",
     ylab = "Density")
lines(density(infection.df$InfctRsk), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```
We can see that there is a minimum somewhere between 1% and 2%, and a maximum is located between 7% and 8%. To explore further, the descriptive statistics for infection risk are shown below. We can see that the minimum infection risk is 1.3%, and the maximum infection risk is 7.8%. The average inflection risk is 4.355%, which matches with the histogram as the density curve peak is between 4% and 5%.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# table of descriptive stats for the inflection risk
statistic <- c("Min", "2nd Quant. (25%)", "Mean","Median", "4th Quant. (75%)", "Max", "StdDev")
data<-infection.df$InfctRsk
quantiles<-quantile(data)
# extracting the number with as.numeric because quantiles[2] is a named number.
second.quant<-as.numeric(quantiles[2])
fourth.quant<-as.numeric(quantiles[4])
mn<-min(data)
mx<-max(data)
avg<-round(mean(data), 2)
md<-median(data)
std<-round(sd(data), 2)
value <- c(mn,second.quant,avg,md,fourth.quant,mx,std)
st.tbl <- cbind(statistic, value)
kable(st.tbl, caption="Infection Risk Descriptive Statistics")

```

## Patient Factors 

The two "Patient" factors in our dataset are Stay and Age. We explored the distributions of these variables.

### The Variable Stay

We first start with the variable Stay, which denotes how long a patient stays at the hospital. 
The histogram's distribution is skewed to the right, with a peak number of patients staying between eight and ten days.We also see that there are some outliers from 16 to 20 days.

From the distribution, we draw the conclusion that patients usually stay at the hospital for less than two weeks, although some patients are outside that range. Most patients may spend about eight to ten days at the hospital. The descriptive statistics tell us that the minimum number of days that a patient stayed at the hospital is 6.7 days, and the maximum number of days that a patient stayed is 19.56 days. The average number of days a patient would stay at the hospital is 9.65 days.

# Modeling 

For our models, infection risk is the dependent variable, and our ten predictors are: "Stay", "Age", "Culture", "Xray", "Beds", "MedSchool", "Region", "Census", "Nurses", and "Facilities".

```{r, include=FALSE}
#Modeling

infection.lm <- lm(
  InfctRsk ~ Stay + Age + Culture + Xray + Beds +
    MedSchool + Region + Census + Nurses + Facilities,
  data = infection.df
)
model.summary <- summary(infection.lm)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#Modeling Results

coefficients <- model.summary$coefficients
coef.tbl <- data.frame(
  Predictor = rownames(coefficients),
  Coefficient = coefficients[, "Estimate"],
  StandardError = coefficients[, "Std. Error"],
  PValue = coefficients[, "Pr(>|t|)"],
  row.names = NULL
)
kable(
  coef.tbl,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Predictor", "Coefficient", "Standard Error", "P-value"),
  caption = "Regression Coefficients and Significance"
)
```
